title: A Power Provider for Meta Urged Regulators to Exempt Data Center Plants From Acid Rain Rules
gist: EPA documents obtained by WIRED show Williams, the gas infrastructure company building at least four ~500MW 'islanded' power plants for Meta data centers in Ohio and Utah, lobbied the EPA (including an 'urgent' meeting request) before the agency's July recommendation to exempt behind-the-meter data-center plants from the Acid Rain Program. Experts say the exemption is legally defensible but erodes SO2/NOx/CO2 emissions reporting just as more than 110GW of behind-the-meter gas projects are planned in the US.

themes.theme: Williams lobbying and the Acid Rain Program exemption

insights.claim: Williams, a gas power provider to several Meta data centers, met with EPA leaders, including then-Air office chief Aaron Szabo, in the run-up to the EPA's July recommendation to waive Acid Rain Program rules for data-center power plants.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Shows gas suppliers to hyperscalers actively shaping deregulation that speeds their behind-the-meter build-out.
insights.locator: Calendar invites provided by EPA show

insights.claim: The EPA in July 2026 recommended that 'islanded' power plants that exclusively power data centers be exempt from the Acid Rain Program because the program was designed for facilities that sell electricity to the grid.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Removes a two-year pre-operation permit requirement, shortening timelines for on-site gas generation at data centers.

insights.claim: Under the Acid Rain Program, covered power plants must submit a permit application two years before coming online and regularly monitor emissions, a timeline Williams called 'not feasible' for urgent AI data-center gas generation.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Permitting lead times are a binding constraint on AI power build-out; their removal favors fast on-site gas developers.
insights.quote: not feasible given the urgent need to install and operate gas-fired generation for AI data centers

insights.claim: Williams was one of three private companies that asked the EPA for guidance on the Acid Rain Program, and its April meeting request to discuss its Ohio and Utah projects for Meta was marked 'urgent'.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Urgency from a key supplier signals Meta's data-center power timelines were at risk from permitting.

insights.claim: Williams first publicly proposed exempting behind-the-meter data centers from the Acid Rain Program in September 2025 House testimony by its then VP Mark Gebbia.

insights.claim: Williams' permit application for its Utah plant serving Meta shows maximum annual emissions of around 100 tons of nitrogen oxide and 11 tons of sulfur dioxide, versus thousands of tons of each for a 500-megawatt coal plant.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Gas plants' lower acid-rain pollutant profile weakens the environmental case against the exemption, lowering regulatory risk.

insights.claim: Exempting data-center power plants from the Acid Rain Program jeopardizes mandatory monitoring and reporting of sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides and carbon dioxide from those plants, especially as the administration moves to repeal separate CO2 reporting.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Less emissions data for AI power reduces transparency for ESG investors and makes data-center carbon footprints harder to verify.

insights.claim: Goffman and Harvard's Carrie Jenks agree the EPA's data-center guidance sticks to the letter of the law, since the 1990 Acid Rain Program was explicitly intended only for plants selling power to the grid, though Earthjustice and the NRDC have challenged the interpretation.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Expert view that the exemption is legally sound reduces near-term litigation risk for behind-the-meter projects.

insights.claim: Carrie Jenks argues Congress should update the law to cover massive behind-the-meter gas plants, since nobody in 1990 envisioned it being economical to build power plants that don't sell their output.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Legislative change is a tail risk that could reimpose permitting costs on off-grid data-center power.
insights.quote: No one expected it to be economical to develop a bunch of power plants that wouldn’t sell the product they were creating.
